crazy_tech: {co} launched a national ID that is also your wallet, your library card and your alibi. Citizens now carry one thing instead of seven, which the government calls simplification and everyone else calls one point of failure. It crashed on launch day, so for a few hours the whole country officially did not exist.
A startup in {town} is replacing the police with an app. You report a crime, rate the response and leave a review. Burglars are already giving it four stars for convenience.

{co} announced a currency backed by nothing, which it describes as 'a bold return to tradition'. Three small countries adopted it as legal tender, mostly because the alternative was also backed by nothing, but with worse branding.
A new bank in {town} charges nothing for accounts and takes a small percentage of your optimism. Customers say the fees feel invisible, which is the whole point of fees.

{co} says its AI can set every price on earth in real time, so inflation will be 'handled'. Economists point out that inflation is just a word for prices doing what prices do. The AI has already raised the price of economists.
A small country has digitised everything: tax, voting, marriage. Citizens report the one thing the new system cannot process is a complaint. 'Error 404: grievance not found,' says the portal.
{co} announced smart traffic lights that talk to each other, and, it turns out, only to each other. Commuters in {town} say the lights have reached an agreement and drivers were not invited.

A security firm will sell every household a drone that circles the block 'for peace of mind'. Neighbours report the peace is unchanged but the minds are more anxious. Squirrels have been reclassified as threats.

{co} is rolling out a payment ring that charges you automatically for anything you pick up, including things you then put back. Shoppers in {town} now walk the aisles with their hands in their pockets like pickpockets in reverse.
A pension app promises 40 percent returns by investing only in things that go up. Regulators asked which things. The app replied, 'The ones that go up.'

{co} announced a global password registry so nobody forgets theirs again. Hackers called it a thoughtful gift. Everyone else has been asked to choose a password they will not use anywhere else, which cannot be done.
Cashless is now law in {town}: no coins, no notes, no excuses. The bus driver says the bus is slower because nobody can find the card. The bakery has begun accepting compliments.
{n} central banks announced a world digital currency at a joint press conference that took four hours and said one sentence. Markets rose, fell and then asked what the sentence was.
{co} will insure your reputation. Premiums rise every time you say something online. Customers in {town} report their reputation is now their most expensive hobby.
A country's power grid now runs on an algorithm that predicts demand from the weather, the news and everyone's mood. It predicted a blackout and caused one, which it calls 'forecast accuracy'.

{co} installed facial recognition across the subway: if you look sad it offers you a coupon, if you look angry it offers you a different train. Commuters say the morning commute has finally become personal.
ridiculous: {co} is selling a plant subscription: you water it through an app, and the plant is plastic. It costs {price} a month, the app reminds you daily, and it needs your photo, your email and a government ID, because plants are apparently a security matter.
A $89 pillow that tells you how badly you slept by sighing at you. It requires an app. Reviewers say the sigh is very realistic.

{co} sells 'premium silence' in a jar for {price}. You open it and nothing happens. Customers say it is the best product they have ever owned, mostly because it is the only thing that stopped talking.
A shoe with a built-in alarm that rings when you are about to make a bad decision. It rings constantly. {price} one-off, no returns, no app, no refunds.
A smartwatch that measures your steps, your heartbeat and your regret. It costs $249, needs a monthly plan and a firmware update, and has never once been wrong about the regret.
A fridge sticker that says the fridge is empty, for people who want to avoid opening it. {price}. Aimed at anyone with a sedentary lifestyle and a strong sense of denial.
{co} sends a monthly box of random cables 'for future needs'. $19 a month, no app, no ID. Customers report an impressive number of cables and no future.
A lifetime membership in a club for people who plan to join a club. {price}. The first meeting is scheduled for next quarter.
An umbrella that costs $140 and only works when it is not raining. Marketed to optimists, sold with a gentle warning.
A wedding ring you rent monthly with 'cancel anytime' flexibility. {price} a month, needs an app and a deeply uncomfortable ID check. Marketed to the committed-ish.
Gold-plated toast, $59 a slice, delivered by a courier who judges you. Needs an app and a phone number, and the courier will ask if you are sure.
{co} sells a 'productivity blanket' that makes you feel like you worked. $79, no app, aimed at people whose calendar is entirely meetings.
Wi-Fi for your pet fish: $9 a month. The fish get no signal, but the owners feel connected. Needs an app and a government ID, because fish are suspicious.
A mirror that compliments you for $15 a month, with a camera that tells you the truth at a discount. The company recommends the compliments.
A $30 annual fee to receive less email. You send the company your email address and it sends you fewer. It works by never replying.
A 'smart' rock: it sits there and learns nothing. {price}. Requires an app, a subscription and a photo of the rock.
sensible: A tool library on {town}'s main street lets you borrow a drill for a day for free. You sign up with a name and phone number and bring it back. It is the most useful thing the town has done in years, and it has no logo.
The bus company is printing timetables that are actually right. They are free at the library, and the driver says he has stopped apologising.
A repair cafe opens on Saturdays: volunteers fix your toaster, your jeans, your bike. It is free, run by retirees, and requires only your toaster.
A neighbours' group offers free rides to the clinic for people who cannot drive. Sign up by phone, a driver arrives, nobody makes a speech.
A $5 monthly service sends you a printed list of everything the council decided this month, in plain words. You can finally stop reading the minutes.
A dentist's office that calls you back. No extra charge, sign up by phone. Patients are said to be in shock.
A shared freezer in {town} where anyone can leave extra food and take some. No app, no ID, no signup: a freezer and trust.
A retired accountant in {town} helps people file their taxes on Tuesdays. Free. Bring your paperwork and a snack. Everyone gets the refund they should always have had.
A $3 monthly 'did anything break' check for elderly neighbours: a volunteer knocks, asks, leaves. You sign up by phone with a name and address. It is the least exciting safety net ever invented.
A community garden rents plots for $20 a season. Sign up in person, no app, and you will mostly get tomatoes and a mild sense of competence.
A walking bus takes kids to school each morning: volunteers walk a line of children from the corner to the gate. Free, sign up at the school office. Parents report spare time.
A monthly street dinner where neighbours cook one big pot, pay what they can and meet each other for the first time in ten years.
local_shock: The only grocery store in {town} will close next month. The owner says the margins disappeared along with the customers who preferred a supermarket twenty minutes away. The town now has a sign that says 'Food' and nothing under it.
{co} will lay off {n} workers at its {town} plant within a week. Nobody was surprised except the people who were told it was 'just a restructuring'. The diner expects its quietest lunch in years.
The bridge to {town} is closed for six months. The detour adds forty minutes. The bridge has been 'under assessment' since a previous mayor, who is also under assessment.

The water in {town} was undrinkable for three days. Officials called it a minor issue, which is what they call issues that are not yet fixed. Bottled water sold out, then returned at double the price.
{town}'s only bank branch is closing and being replaced by an app and a very small sign. Seniors say the app does not do cash, handshakes or being asked how their knee is.

The high school in {town} is moving to a four-day week to save money. Parents are happy, teachers are tired, and the teenagers say they will spend the fifth day on 'self-directed learning', which they have already renamed sleep.
A heat wave knocked out power in {town} for two days. The one cold drink in the shop cost $9. The town is now suspicious of anything with a plug.
A lottery winner in {town} won $40 million and immediately bought the only hardware store, then closed it. Locals are split between delight and an urgent need for screws.

The volunteer fire department in {town} has no volunteers left. The chief says the trucks are fine; it is the humans who got old. The council has promised a 'review', which is how councils say 'later'.
A scandal in {town}: the mayor's brother ran the contract for the new streetlights, which are on at noon and off at midnight. The mayor said the lights were 'strategic'.
The annual festival in {town} was cancelled because the insurance cost more than the fireworks. The town held it anyway, with a few sparklers and a man shouting.
{town}'s maternity ward is closing. Expectant mothers will now drive ninety minutes. The hospital calls it a 'consolidation', a word that means somewhere else.
A new landlord bought half of {town} and raised rents by {pct} percent. He said he was 'responding to the market', which is what landlords say after talking to themselves.
The one bus route in {town} has been cut. Residents say they now walk, hitchhike or grow very close to their neighbours, whichever comes first.
policy: The government announced a ban on cash payments over ten dollars 'to fight crime'. Criminals expressed concern about their retirement plans. Grandmothers asked what to do with the jar.
A new law caps bank fees but allows 'administrative adjustments'. Banks say the new charges are called adjustments, not fees, which is a relief to everyone who loves vocabulary.
A national four-day working week begins next year for everyone except the people who announced it. Employers say they will 'adapt', which in practice means five days of work in four.
The government is taxing bottled water at ten percent 'for the environment'. The environment said it had not asked. Tap water is being rebranded as 'artisan'.
A new rule requires every social app to show a warning: 'this will waste your time'. The apps say it is fine. Users say they will read it later.
A 20 mph limit was imposed on all city streets. Drivers say the city is now a parking lot with ambitions. Cyclists are suing the cars for being slower.
A new law makes landlords publish the real condition of every rental. Landlords call it harassment. Tenants call it Tuesday.
The pension age is rising by two years 'to reflect longer lives'. Citizens point out that the extra two years will be spent waiting for a pension.
A tipping law abolishes tipping and raises menu prices by 20 percent. Waiters are happy, diners are confused, and the tip jar has been moved to a museum.
A privacy law requires every company to explain what it does with your data in one sentence. Companies are working on the sentence. It is currently six pages.
Gig workers will now get sick pay, holiday pay and a pension. Platforms say the apps will cost more. Customers are reminded the apps already cost more.
Airlines must now refund delayed flights within 14 days. The airlines said the deadline is 'aspirational'. Passengers said the word was aspirational too.
macro: A key shipping lane is closed after an accident, and ships are going the long way round. Prices for everything that arrives by ship, which is everything, are set to rise. Experts blame 'unforeseen circumstances', the circumstances nobody forecasts and everybody has.
A heat wave cut wheat exports from three countries at once, and bread prices are rising in forty. Politicians are asking people to remain calm and eat less toast.
A cyberattack froze payments across a dozen banks for six hours. Cash, previously declared dead, enjoyed a brief and dignified resurrection.

A major chip factory stopped production after a power failure. Cars, phones and fridges are waiting. The world is learning that its entire future depends on one building with a very good air conditioner.
An oil producer cut output without telling its customers. Fuel prices rose in thirty countries. Governments blamed each other, and then the weather.
A new AI model was released that can write reports, laws and apologies. Governments say it will help. Lawyers say they will bill more. The apologies were judged the most believable.
A bank run in a mid-size country spread overnight to its neighbours. Savers queued, central banks reassured, and a rumour did most of the work.
An undersea internet cable was cut. Streaming slowed across a continent, and for the first time in years people discovered what the evening looks like.
A trade treaty between two giants was signed after eleven years. Tariffs fall, prices wobble, and thirty lobbyists get a very good lunch.
A pandemic scare closed borders for four days, then reopened them 'with new guidance'. Airlines gained the guidance, passengers gained the delay.
A melting glacier flooded a mountain valley and cut a trade route. Three countries argued about who owns the water, and a fourth started selling bottled air.
An election in a very large country has made currency traders very busy and everyone else very tired. Markets called it 'a pivotal moment', which is what they call every moment.
